transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so, I guess the main thing that finally pushed me to come in today—which, honestly, took me a few weeks to actually call and set up—is work. I work as an insurance claims clerk, so I'm processing policies, checking data, making sure everything matches up for the adjusters. It's a lot of screen time, obviously. 

But the big issue is that I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. And I know I’m supposed to stay put and finish my claim reviews. We have this queue, right? A certain number of claims we have to get through, and my supervisor tracks our metrics pretty closely. But I’ll be sitting there, maybe halfway through a really standard auto policy review, and suddenly I’m just... I'm out of my chair. I’m walking to the breakroom to check the fridge even though I just ate, or I'm going to the bathroom for the fifth time, or just wandering over to the printer when I haven't even printed anything. 

I know I need to just sit there and grind through the reviews, but it's like my brain just decides we're done sitting. My boss has started making these little comments about how I'm never at my desk when he walks by, and it's just getting really frustrating because I want to just do the work and keep my job, you know? I dropped out of college a few years ago so I really need this job to work out, but I just... I can't seem to just stay in the chair.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you are sitting at your desk?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, when I actually *am* at my desk, it's not like I'm just sitting there perfectly still. It's almost worse when we have those mandatory training sessions or the longer team meetings, you know? Like, we had this one last week about a new software update for the claims portal, and it was supposed to be an hour, but it dragged on to almost an hour and a half because people kept asking questions about the drop-down menus. And I was just... I mean, I'm sitting there, and I know my supervisor is two rows back, so I'm really trying to look focused and professional, making eye contact with the presenter, all that stuff. 

But my leg is just going a mile a minute under the table. Like, constantly bouncing. And if I force myself to stop the leg bouncing, then I realize I'm clicking my pen. Click, click, click. I had a coworker actually turn around once and give me this look, so I put the pen down, but then I'm just shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. It's like the energy has to go somewhere. Even when I'm just at my own workstation, looking at a screen, I'm tapping my foot on the leg of the desk or twisting around in my chair. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to keep it all contained when I'm supposed to just be sitting quietly and paying attention.
Did you have trouble sitting still or paying attention when you were a kid?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, definitely. I mean, looking back, this whole thing... it isn't exactly brand new for me. Like, I remember my mom keeping all my old report cards from elementary school in this big plastic tub in the basement, and we looked through them a few years ago when I was moving out. And it was just, like, a running theme every single year. My teachers would always write the exact same kind of stuff in the little comments section at the bottom. 

They’d always start with something nice, you know, like, "He's very bright," or "He grasps the concepts quickly." But then there was always a "but." It was always, "but he loses his worksheets," or "he forgets to turn in his homework even when it's done in his folder." Which was so true, I used to just shove papers into my backpack until they were completely crumpled. And they'd write about how I missed instructions all the time. Like, the teacher would explain the whole math assignment, and I’d be staring out the window at a bird or something, and then I’d have to ask the kid next to me what we were supposed to be doing. 

And finishing classwork was a whole other thing. They always noted that I needed constant reminders to just finish what was right in front of me. Like, we'd have 20 minutes of silent reading or worksheet time, and I'd do the first two questions, and then I'd start drawing on the margins, or taking my eraser apart, or trying to balance my pencil on my finger. The teacher would have to walk by and tap my desk, like, three times before recess just to get me to finish. So, yeah, it’s always been there, just... I guess the consequences are a lot bigger now that it's a job and not a spelling worksheet, you know?
Have you ever acted on impulse, doing something without fully thinking it through?

Um, no, not really. I mean, when you say "acting on impulse," I think of people who, like, jump out of planes or suddenly buy a sports car or, I don't know, quit their job in a blaze of glory or something. And that's definitely not me. I'm actually pretty risk-averse, all things considered. 

Like, even when I dropped out of college, it wasn't this sudden, impulsive decision where I just woke up one day and said, "I'm done." It was this long, drawn-out process of failing classes and agonizing over it and talking to my parents—well, trying to talk to my parents, they didn't really get it—but it wasn't a snap judgment. And with my job now, even though I'm struggling with the sitting still and the focus, I'm not doing anything crazy. I'm not yelling at my boss or sending inappropriate emails or doing things without thinking about the consequences. I worry about the consequences constantly, honestly. 

I might get distracted, sure, or I might, you know, walk away from my desk when I shouldn't, but it's not like a dangerous impulse or a wild decision. It's just my brain kind of drifting off. So, no, I wouldn't say I do things without thinking them through first. If anything, I probably overthink things, especially when it comes to work and making sure I don't mess up a claim, because the adjusters get really annoyed if the data isn't perfect, and then it comes back on me, and then my supervisor gets involved, and it's just a whole thing. So yeah, no big impulsive actions here.
Do you have trouble focusing or following through on instructions at home, like when you're doing chores or personal projects?

Um, I don't know if I'd say I have trouble following through on instructions at home, because, well, it's just me there, so nobody's really giving me instructions, you know? Like, I live alone in this one-bedroom apartment over in the West End, and I guess I make my own rules, so it's not like work where there's a strict procedure for everything. But if you mean just getting stuff done around the house... I mean, I guess I do okay? 

I don't really have any big personal projects going on right now. I thought about getting into woodworking a couple of years ago, bought a few starter tools, but they're just sitting in the closet because my apartment doesn't really have the space for a workbench, and the noise would probably drive my downstairs neighbor crazy. He already complained once when I was putting together an IKEA bookshelf at, like, 11 PM, which, fair enough, I shouldn't have been hammering that late. But anyway, as far as chores go... I mean, the dishes get done eventually. The laundry gets done when I start running out of clean shirts for work. I wouldn't say I have a hard time with it, it's just normal life stuff, right? Everyone puts off vacuuming until they absolutely have to. I don't think I struggle with it any more than the next guy. I just kind of do things when they need to be done.
Do you have difficulty organizing your time or daily activities outside of work?

Well, outside of work... I mean, I guess I kind of just touched on that, right? Like, at home, things are pretty low-stakes. But if you're asking about organizing my time in general, I think where it really, really hits me is actually back at work, to be honest. I know you asked about outside of work, but my brain just immediately goes to my desk because that's where the wheels completely fall off. 

Like, recently, they bumped up my caseload. We had a couple of people leave the department—one guy moved to underwriting, and another lady retired—so they distributed their accounts among the rest of us. And ever since that happened, my desk is just... it's a disaster zone. I've got physical claim folders stacked up, but not in any logical order. It's just like, a pile of auto claims here, some property damage ones over there, and then I've got sticky notes stuck to the edges of my monitor, on the bezel, you know? And half the time the sticky notes lose their stickiness and fall onto the keyboard, and I don't even know which file they were supposed to go with. 

And my inbox is even worse. I try to use the little red flags in Outlook, but then I end up flagging everything, so the flags mean nothing. I'll have fifty flagged emails, and when I sit down in the morning with my coffee, I just stare at the screen. I literally have no idea which policy review I'm supposed to tackle first. Should I do the oldest one? The one with the highest payout? The one from the adjuster who called and yelled at me yesterday? I spend so much time just trying to figure out where to start that I end up wasting an hour just clicking between different windows and shuffling folders around. So, yeah, organizing my time and my tasks... it's a huge, huge struggle, but mostly when I have all these competing priorities at the office. At home, if I don't organize my time, I just end up watching YouTube for three hours, which isn't great, but it doesn't get me written up, you know?
Do you often feel anxious or stressed about not meeting your work expectations or making mistakes on the job?

Oh, man, anxious doesn't even begin to cover it. I am constantly stressed about it. Constantly. Like, I wake up in the middle of the night thinking about whether I attached the right police report to a file, or if I missed a deadline on a subrogation demand. And, honestly, it's not just in my head anymore, because it's actually happening. My supervisor, Brenda—she's usually pretty chill, but she had to pull me into a one-on-one meeting last week, and she officially put me on performance coaching. 

And that just... it just crushed me, honestly. Because we sat down, and she pulled up my metrics on her screen, and she was pointing out how my claim files are falling way behind the department average. And she started questioning my accuracy, too, which is the worst part, because I try so hard to get it right. She showed me a couple of files where I'd transposed numbers in the VIN or missed a coverage limit in the policy docs. And she was like, "We need to see immediate improvement here," and gave me this whole formal action plan with weekly check-ins. 

So now I have this massive knot in my stomach every time I log in. I was really, really hoping to get on the senior adjuster track by the end of the year—that was my whole goal, you know? It comes with a pay bump, and you get to do field work sometimes instead of just staring at a screen all day, which I think would be so much better for me. But now? With this performance coaching thing on my record and my accuracy being questioned, I'm terrified I'm going to lose that opportunity completely. Or worse, you know, lose the job entirely if I can't figure out how to keep all these details straight. It's just so much pressure, and I feel like I'm drowning in it every single day.
Did you experience significant difficulties with restlessness, inattention, or impulsivity as a child, aside from what you've already mentioned about school?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because with all this stuff happening at work with Brenda and the performance coaching, it really got me thinking about when I was younger. Because, honestly, looking back... this whole thing with missing details and falling behind? It's not actually brand new for me. Like, I remember back in elementary school—specifically, I think it was third or fourth grade, Mrs. Gable's class, she had this whole system with color-coded folders that was supposed to keep us organized, but it just completely backfired for me. 

My parents actually kept a bunch of my old report cards in this big plastic bin in their basement, and I was looking through them a while ago. And it's almost comical, really, because every single year, the comments from the teachers were practically identical. They'd always start with something nice, like, "He's a bright boy," or "He contributes great ideas during group discussions," but then there was always the "but." It was always, "but he loses his worksheets," or "he has trouble keeping track of his assignments." 

I remember I would shove papers into my desk instead of putting them in my backpack, and by the end of the semester, my desk was just a crumpled, overflowing mess of half-finished math sheets and spelling tests. And the teachers were constantly writing notes home saying that I missed instructions. Like, they'd explain a project, and I'd be looking right at them, but my brain was just... somewhere else, maybe thinking about a book I was reading or staring at a bug on the window. And then everyone would start working, and I'd just be sitting there, completely lost, having to ask the kid next to me what we were supposed to be doing. 

And the reminders... oh man, the reminders. They always wrote that I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork. I'd start a worksheet, get through the first three questions, and then just drift off. The teacher would have to come tap on my desk and say, "Hey, focus, let's get this done." So, yeah, the restlessness and the impulsivity, I don't know if I was bouncing off the walls or anything, but the inattention? The losing things and missing instructions? That was definitely there. It's just wild to me that I'm basically dealing with the adult version of the exact same thing now with my claim files and my inbox. It's like I never really grew out of it, you know? Just swapped out math worksheets for insurance policies.
Are your symptoms affecting your relationships with friends or family?

Friends or family? Um... you know, honestly, no, I don't really think so. Not that I've noticed, anyway. 

Like, my parents, for example—they live about forty minutes away, out in the suburbs, and we usually do a family dinner maybe every other Sunday. And sure, maybe I'll forget to text my mom back right away if she sends me a link to an article or asks if I'm bringing anything to dinner, but she's so used to it by now. I mean, like I said with the whole report card thing, she was the one dealing with my messy folders and missing homework back in elementary school, so she knows exactly how I am. She just kind of laughs it off and says, "Oh, you know how he gets." So there's no real friction there. My dad's pretty laid back, too, so they don't get mad at me for being a little scattered.

And then with my friends... I mean, my social circle is pretty small these days anyway. It’s mostly just a couple of guys I went to college with before I stopped taking classes. Like my buddy Mark, we usually just hop on Discord and play video games on the weekends. And the great thing about that is, there's no real schedule or pressure, you know? If I completely zone out during a match and get sniped, nobody is pulling up my metrics or putting me on a formal action plan for it. It's just casual. Or if we make plans to grab a beer at this place downtown we like, and I show up fifteen minutes late because I spent twenty minutes looking for my keys—which happens constantly, I swear they just vanish into thin air the second I walk into my apartment—Mark really doesn't care. Half the time he's running late himself. 

So, yeah, I feel like my personal relationships are actually the one area of my life where I'm doing okay right now. Because my friends and family don't expect me to organize files or process fifty auto claims a day, they just want to hang out. The stakes are just so much lower. So, no, it's not really causing any drama or fights or anything like that with them. It really is just the work stuff that's completely burying me.
Are you having trouble completing daily tasks or activities outside of work due to your symptoms?

Outside of work? Um... honestly, I don't even really know, because my brain is just so completely consumed by the daily tasks I'm messing up *at* work. Like, I get home and I'm just obsessing over my desk and my files, so the home stuff doesn't even really register. I just kind of crash. 

Because... well, when it comes to those daily tasks, I forget simple work follow-ups way, way more than I want to admit. To you, to Brenda, to anyone. It’s always the little routine things, you know? Like returning a claimant’s call. A claimant will leave a voicemail—maybe they're asking if their rental car extension got approved, or if we received their police report—and I'll listen to it, write their claim number on a pink sticky note, and tell myself, "Okay, I'm going to call them back the exact second I finish reading this policy document." But then I get a new email, or I have to look up a state statute for a different file, and suddenly it's five o'clock and I completely forgot they even called. I'll find the sticky note stuck to the bottom of my stapler three days later.

And updating diary notes! That's another huge one. Our software has this diary system where you're supposed to log every single action you take on a claim. You touch a file, you make a diary note, that's the golden rule of adjusting. But I'll read through an entire fifty-page medical record, figure out exactly what needs to happen next, and then just... close the window without actually updating the diary note. I just move on to the next thing. So Brenda or whoever looks at the file, and it looks like I haven't done a single thing on it in two weeks, even though I did the work! 

Or, like, sending a form I meant to send earlier that day. I'll literally have a property damage release PDF generated, sitting right there open on my screen. I'll even start drafting the email to the body shop, but then someone pings me on Teams with a question, and the draft just sits there minimized. I won't even realize I never actually attached the form and hit send until the shop calls me the next morning yelling about how they can't start repairs. 

So, yeah, I don't know about outside of work, but the daily tasks for my job? It's just this constant, exhausting cycle of forgetting these basic follow-ups and then scrambling to fix them before it blows up in my face.
Are there any daily activities you enjoy doing in your free time that you've had to stop or reduce because of your difficulties with focus or restlessness?

Stop doing things I enjoy? Um... no, honestly, I don't think so. It’s actually kind of the opposite, really? Like, I still do all the stuff I like to do, mostly because... well, when I'm doing something I actually *want* to do, or something that's just for fun, the focus thing doesn't seem to ruin it the same way it does with my claim files. 

Like I mentioned earlier with my buddy Mark and the video games. We play a lot of shooters, or sometimes these big open-world games, and honestly, I can sit there for four hours straight on a Saturday and not even realize what time it is. Which is crazy, right? Because I can't look at a two-page police report at my desk for five minutes without my brain wanting to just completely eject out of my skull. But with a game, there's always something happening, you know? There's something flashing, or a new objective popping up on the screen, or Mark is yelling in my headset about someone flanking us, so my brain is just constantly getting fed whatever it needs to stay locked in. I don't even have time to zone out. 

And as for the restlessness... I mean, I don't really get that physically anyway, like I'm not needing to go run a marathon or pace around the block. When I get home from the office, I'm just so completely mentally fried from trying to keep my head above water with Brenda and this whole performance plan that I basically just melt into my couch. I'll pull up YouTube and start watching one video about, I don't know, how they restore old cast iron skillets, and then my brain just latches onto it and suddenly it's midnight and I've watched twenty consecutive videos on historical blacksmithing techniques. 

So I definitely haven't had to give up my free time stuff. If anything, the free time stuff is the only thing keeping me sane right now, because there's no penalty if I miss a tiny detail or if I do happen to zone out for a second. Nobody is grading me on how well I watch a movie. It's just... easy. The pressure is off. So, yeah, no, I haven't had to stop doing anything fun. It's really just the work stuff that's the nightmare.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like your symptoms are causing significant problems or distress for you?

Oh, God, yes. I mean, like I've been hinting at this whole time, it's work. It's 100% work. That is the area of my life that is just... it's a complete disaster area right now, and the distress is honestly off the charts. I wake up in the morning and my stomach is already tied in knots just thinking about logging in and looking at my queue. 

Because, well, I know I mentioned Brenda earlier—she's my supervisor—and she actually just officially put me on performance coaching. Which, if you don't know the corporate insurance world, is basically this giant, blinking neon warning sign right before things get really bad. She sat me down last week and we had this whole agonizing meeting about how my claim files are just completely falling behind. I'm missing deadlines, I'm sitting on files that should have been closed out days ago, and it's piling up. 

And it's not even just the speed or the volume, which is bad enough, but my accuracy is being seriously questioned now, too. Like, I'll miss a single digit on a VIN number, or I'll accidentally apply a five-hundred-dollar deductible to a non-fault collision claim because I just completely glossed over the subrogation notes, and then the whole file is just messed up and has to be flagged and audited. So now Brenda is basically breathing down my neck, double-checking everything I touch. 

And the absolute worst part—the thing that really just keeps me up at night and makes me feel sick to my stomach—is that I was actually aiming for this senior adjuster track. I've been working toward it since I got hired. It comes with a better salary, obviously, but you also get to handle more complex liability cases instead of just churning through hundreds of these minor, mind-numbing fender benders every week. I really, really wanted it. I thought I could do it. But now? With this coaching plan and my files looking like a bomb went off in them, I am so incredibly worried that I'm going to completely lose my shot at that track. Like, they're obviously not going to hand a senior promotion to the guy who can't even remember to attach a PDF or update a diary note, you know? It's embarrassing. So, yeah, the distress is huge. It feels like I'm watching my career just slip right through my fingers and I can't stop it.
Are there any situations outside of work where you feel like your symptoms are causing problems for you?

Outside of work? Causing problems? Um... I mean, honestly, no. I really don't think so. 

Like I was saying before, my life outside the office is pretty much just... recovering from the office. I don't really have a lot of high-stakes stuff going on in my personal life that I *could* mess up, you know? Like, I share an apartment with this guy Dave, we went to college together for a bit, and we basically just keep to ourselves. If I forget to take the trash out on Tuesday night, or if I leave a cereal bowl on the coffee table for two days because I just got distracted and walked away from it... Dave just doesn't care. Or he just takes the trash out himself. Nobody is writing me up for a missed trash day, you know? There’s no... there's no 'chore performance plan' in my apartment. So there's no real friction or problems there. 

And socially, my friends are all just super laid back. If I forget to text Mark back about grabbing a beer or something, he just hops on Discord later and yells at me through the headset anyway. It's not like with Brenda, where if I miss a message, it's this catastrophic failure of my duties as a claims clerk and suddenly my whole career is in jeopardy. 

So, yeah, I don't feel like I'm having any real problems outside of work at all. The distress is just entirely, 100 percent compartmentalized to my desk and my queue. When I'm home, I'm just... existing. The pressure is totally off, and the things I do mess up just don't matter. So, no, I really can't think of anything outside the office that's actually causing me any grief right now.
Are there any daily activities outside of work that you feel you're not doing as well as you used to because of your symptoms?

Activities outside of work? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on what you count as a daily activity, right? Because like I was saying, my life outside the office isn't exactly demanding. I don't have kids, I don't have a mortgage, I'm not, like, building a deck on the weekends or doing anything that requires a lot of sustained mental energy. My routine is basically just... wake up, commute, survive the eight hours of absolute misery at my desk, and then come home and decompress. 

So if you mean things like chores... I guess you could look at my laundry or cooking or something? But Dave and I have lived like this since we were in the dorms together, so my standards for "doing well" at home are just incredibly low. If I throw all my clothes into the washer in one giant load on cold and actually remember to move them to the dryer before they get that weird mildew smell, that's a win for me. I'm not separating colors or ironing shirts, I'm just surviving. I usually just order takeout or make frozen pizzas, too, so there's really no metric for me to fail at when it comes to cooking, either. 

And with my hobbies, like the gaming with Mark or the YouTube rabbit holes I mentioned, I'm doing those exactly the same as I always have. It's not like my aim in a shooter game has gotten worse, or I'm somehow bad at watching videos. If anything, I'm probably leaning into those things way more now just to escape the stress from the performance plan stuff at work. I mean, I guess I used to go to the gym a little more back when I was taking classes, but stopping that isn't really a focus thing or me not doing it well, it's just an exhaustion thing. By the time I log off and get away from Brenda's micromanaging and all those audited files, my brain is just total mush. I don't have the energy to go lift weights. 

So, yeah, I really don't think there's any specific task or hobby outside of the office where I sit back and think, "Wow, I'm really slipping here." The slipping is completely, one hundred percent contained to Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM. Outside of that time frame, I'm just coasting, and you don't really need to be focused to just... coast, you know?
Are there any aspects of your daily life outside of work where you feel your symptoms are significantly interfering with your ability to function?

I mean... I feel like I’m kind of repeating myself a bit here, but honestly, the answer is still just no. 

When you say "interfering with my ability to function," I guess you have to look at what functioning actually looks like for me outside the office. Like, what is there to even interfere with, you know? I pay my half of the rent, sure, but Dave and I have that set up on auto-pay through the apartment building's online portal. I don't even have to think about it, the money just magically vanishes from my checking account on the first of the month. And as for keeping myself alive and fed? I mean, I have the UberEats and DoorDash apps right on my phone's home screen. I probably spend way too much money on delivery fees, honestly—Dave actually gives me a hard time about it because the markups are getting completely insane lately—but it’s just so easy and it requires zero mental effort. 

So as far as actually failing to function? No. Because my entire life outside of that insurance office is basically engineered to be completely frictionless. I deliberately don’t put myself in situations where I *have* to function at some high, demanding level. If I had to, I don't know, organize a neighborhood block party or manage a little league team or juggle a bunch of different volunteer committees, then yeah, maybe I'd be dropping the ball left and right. But I don't do any of that. My weekend is literally just me, my PC, and trying to scrub the memory of Brenda's agonizing performance coaching meetings out of my brain before Monday morning rolls around and I have to do it all over again. 

So, yeah, no. There's no interference with my functioning because, outside of work, there are basically zero expectations placed on me. It's just downtime.
Are there any areas of your personal life where you feel like you're struggling more now than you used to?

I mean... Doc, I know you keep asking about my personal life, and I'm really trying to think if there's something I'm missing, but... no. It really isn't my personal life where I'm struggling more. Like I said, everything at home with Dave and my friends is just exactly the same as it's always been. But work? Work is where everything is just completely falling apart right now. That's the real struggle. That's honestly the whole reason I'm even talking to you today. 

Because, see, Brenda—my supervisor, who I was talking about earlier—she actually officially put me on this performance coaching plan. Which, you know, sounds like it's supposed to be this positive, helpful thing, right? "Coaching." But it's really just corporate speak for a documented paper trail of how badly I'm messing up. My claim files are just falling so far behind the daily quota we're supposed to hit, and it just keeps piling up. And then, even on the ones I do manage to push through the system, she's pulling me aside and constantly questioning my accuracy. Like, I'll miss some tiny detail on a policy rider, or I'll forget to check a specific box on a liability form because I was trying to rush to catch up, and suddenly it's this huge ordeal where we have to have a "touch base" meeting about my attention to detail. 

And the thing that's really stressing me out, the thing that's just completely eating at me every single day, is that I was actually really aiming for the senior adjuster track. I've been working toward that for a while now, and it's a pretty big deal. It comes with a decent pay bump, better hours, and you get to handle more complex cases instead of just mindlessly processing the basic, mind-numbing fender-benders all day long. But now? With this performance plan and Brenda constantly looking over my shoulder, auditing my queues, and pulling me into these meetings... I'm just incredibly worried that I could lose that senior adjuster track entirely. I mean, they're obviously not going to promote the guy who can't even keep his basic entry-level files accurate and on time, right? 

So, if we're talking about where I'm struggling more now than I used to... it's absolutely that. It's the fact that I'm watching this promotion I really wanted just slip away because I can't seem to get my brain to cooperate with these claim files. It's all happening right there at that desk, not in my personal life.
Are there any areas of your daily life outside of work where you feel like you're unable to perform tasks as you normally would?

I mean, Doc, I feel like I'm going a little crazy here, or maybe we're just talking past each other, but... I really, truly don't know how else to answer this. The answer is still just no. I’m not trying to be difficult, I promise, I’m just... I feel like I’m a broken record at this point. 

There are no tasks outside of work that I’m suddenly unable to do, because my normal life outside of work doesn't actually involve any real tasks. Like, what are we even talking about here? Doing the dishes? Dave and I just use paper plates half the time anyway because neither of us wants to deal with loading the dishwasher. So I can't exactly fail at that. Vacuuming? I think we run the vacuum maybe once a month, and it takes ten minutes. My "normal" is just so incredibly low-stakes that there is absolutely no room for me to be unable to perform it. I'm not, you know, trying to restore a classic car in my garage or manage a stock portfolio or anything that requires any actual brainpower. 

My normal is just surviving the absolute gauntlet of my claims queue, getting lectured by Brenda because I missed a checkbox on a liability form, and then coming home, ordering food, and staring at a screen until I fall asleep. And I am still perfectly capable of ordering food and staring at a screen. I haven't lost a step there at all. So, yeah, I really don't have anything else to give you on this one. It's just work. It's only work. Everything else is exactly the same as it's always been.
Are you experiencing any significant distress or problems in your relationships with friends or family due to your symptoms?

Okay, I... look, Doc, I really don't want to sound like a jerk here, but I genuinely feel like we are just looping. I know you have to ask these things, but... no. No, zero distress. Zero problems with my friends or my family. 

I mean, I already told you about Dave. Dave and I have lived together for three years now. He works in IT, he's in his room half the time, I'm in mine.
